facts: The total area under a normal curve is $1$, because every value of the variable lies somewhere under the curve.
The curve is symmetrical about the mean, so the mean, the median and the mode all sit at $x=\mu$.
The **global maximum** is the peak at $x=\mu$; the curve falls away on both sides and never reaches the horizontal axis.
The **points of inflection**, where the curve stops bending downwards and starts bending upwards, are at $\mu-\sigma$ and $\mu+\sigma$.
Changing $\mu$ slides the whole curve left or right along the axis without changing its shape.
A larger $\sigma$ spreads the curve wider, and since the area stays $1$ the peak must become lower.
A smaller $\sigma$ makes the curve narrower and taller, with the values packed more tightly around the mean.
A context suits a normal model when its values are continuous, cluster about one centre, and fall away evenly on both sides.

foundation.question_text: The masses of a large sample of newborn babies are recorded. Explain whether a normal random variable is a reasonable model for this context.
foundation.solution_text:
Mass is a continuous quantity, so it can take any value in a range.
Most newborns have a mass close to the middle of the range, and the numbers of unusually light and unusually heavy babies fall away at about the same rate on each side.
Yes, a normal random variable is a reasonable model.

development.question_text: Customers at a help desk wait a mean of $4$ minutes, but a small number of them wait more than $30$ minutes. Explain whether a normal random variable is a reasonable model for the waiting times.
development.solution_text:
A normal curve is symmetrical about its mean, so values far above the mean must be as common as values the same distance below it.
A wait of $30$ minutes is $26$ minutes above the mean, but a wait $26$ minutes below the mean is impossible.
The long tail on the right makes the distribution skewed, so a normal random variable is not a reasonable model.

development.question_text: Two normal curves are drawn on the same axes and have the same mean. One has a peak height of $0.4$ and the other has a peak height of $0.2$. Explain which curve has the larger standard deviation.
development.solution_text:
Each curve encloses a total area of $1$.
The curve with the peak height of $0.2$ is only half as tall, so it must be spread over a wider interval to enclose the same area.
The curve with the peak height of $0.2$ has the larger standard deviation.

mastery.question_text: $X$ has mean $60$ and standard deviation $5$. $Y$ has the same mean, and the points of inflection of its curve are twice as far from the mean as those of $X$. State the standard deviation of $Y$ and compare the peak heights of the two curves.
mastery.solution_text:
The points of inflection of $X$ are at $60\pm 5$, so those of $Y$ are at $60\pm 10$.
$\sigma_Y$
$=2\times 5$
$=10$
The area under each curve is $1$, and the curve of $Y$ is spread over twice the width.
The peak of $Y$ is lower than the peak of $X$.

mastery.question_text: A student draws two normal curves on one set of axes, one with $\sigma=4$ and one with $\sigma=8$, and makes the two peaks the same height. Explain why the drawing must be wrong.
mastery.solution_text:
Every normal curve encloses a total area of $1$.
The curve with $\sigma=8$ is twice as spread out as the curve with $\sigma=4$, so it covers roughly twice the width of the axis.
If it also had the same peak height, it would enclose about twice the area, and both areas cannot equal $1$.
The wider curve must have the lower peak, so the drawing is wrong.
